Title: A MUSE NFM exploration of the youngest externally photoevaporated planet forming disks in NGC2024
Abstract: Strong evidences that the Solar System formed nearby high-mass stars clash with the observations that planet forming disks in these environments survive such a short time, that planet formation could be completely suppressed. Here we want to test the hypothesis that there is enough time to form the planets if they are shielded by interstellar extinction for the first 0.5-1 Myr of their life. Instead of studying the already optically revealed but 1-3 Myr old Orion Nebula Cluster, we turn to its younger (0.5 Myr) nearby twin, NGC2024, the "Flame Nebula". Only the sensitivity and technical capability to AO-correct the IFS observations of MUSE NFM can for the first time unveal the surroundings of disks in this still embedded region. Building upon pioneering HST and JWST observations, we study the only 8 photoevaporated disks observable in this region. We will measure their mass loss rates and combine them to their ALMA-based disk masses, to firmly assess the time they have to form planets.

Title: Does Late Infall Regulate Disk Accretion?
Abstract: A major uncertainty in star and planet formation is whether protoplanetary disks evolve in isolation or remain connected to their local environment. Corona Australis (CrA) offers a unique test: most disks in its young CrA-Main population show extended structures associated with late infall of ambient material. We propose VLT/X-Shooter observations to obtain an unbiased census of mass accretion rates in CrA-Main, complementing a newly approved ALMA survey of the entire disk population designed to identify and characterize late infall. We will test whether accretion rates depends on local cloud density, whether disks undergoing infall have distinct accretion depletion timescales, and whether stellar accretion rate is linked to the infall rate. Together, X-Shooter and ALMA will connect environment, infall, disk properties, and stellar accretion across an entire Class II population, determining whether late infall actively regulates planet-forming disks.

Title: Does Late Infall Reset Dust Evolution in Class II Disks?
Abstract: Class II disks are usually treated as isolated reservoirs, yet growing evidence shows that some remain connected to their natal environment and undergo renewed external accretion. Such late infall may replenish disk mass and deliver new solids available for planet formation. We propose SPHERE I and H band polarimetry of eight spiral disks spanning active infall, streamer disk interaction, post-infall candidates, and an internally perturbed control. Accurate polarized reflectivity and their ratio,   and the degrees of polarization, interpreted with radiative transfer models, will constrain the size and aggregate structure of micron-sized grains. Trends across the gas evidence selected sequence, together with spatial comparisons within disks will test how delivered grains evolve, where they are processed, and how rapidly their signature is erased. This program will provide the first systematic dust-based test of late infall during the Class II phase.

Title: Hunting for Architectures across the Ridge: Kinematics and Orbital Network of Nomadic Exo-Neptunes (HARKONNEN)
Abstract:
Most of the known exoplanet population consists of close-in worlds orbiting within 30 days around their star. Among them, Neptunes stand out by their diversity in internal structure and strikingly structured demographics. The ridge, an over-occurrence of Neptunes separating a barren desert at short periods from a midly populated savanna at longer periods, represents a transition region where multiple process coexist. This makes ridge Neptunes, together with the few desert Neptunes, targets of high-interest to investigate these processes, whose interplay and relative contributions remain poorly constrained. In particular, determining the fraction of close-in Neptunes originating from late high-eccentricity migration (HEM) versus early disk-driven migration (DDM) in the ridge, or from hot Jupiters undergoing Roche-lobe overflow in the desert, is essential to understand their overall atmospheric evolution. Because these scenarios yield distinct orbital architectures, obliquity (the angle between stellar spin and planetary orbital normal) is a critical observational tracer to differentiate them. 

We therefore propose HARKONNEN, a homogeneous census of 36 Neptunes' obliquities within a volume-limited sample covering the ridge and unexplored desert. The combination of the VLT large collecting area, ESPRESSO high spectral resolution, and high-sensitivity of the Rossiter-McLaughlin Revolutions technique will enable measuring their obliquity  to a precision better than 30 deg (with an average of 15 deg over the sample). Combining these measurements with dedicated stellar photometric monitoring will allow us to derive the 3D orbital architectures of the systems and statistically reconstruct the distributions of aligned and misaligned Neptunes, assessing in particular the debated presence of a polar cluster that would reveal missing dynamical processes. 

We will interpret the measured obliquities jointly with planetary, stellar, and companion properties, using statistical analyses and secular evolutionary models coupling the competing dynamical and atmospheric processes. This approach will constrain the relative contributions of DDM and HEM, and their interplay with post-migration processes, allowing us to build a unified picture of close-in Neptune evolution. HARKONNEN offers timely complementarity to the JWST and upcoming PLATO mission, linking inner orbital architectures with the broader system architectures explored by PLATO and atmospheric compositions characterized with the JWST, and thus connecting the present-day properties of close-in Neptunes to their formation conditions beyond the ice line. At minimum, HARKONNEN will substantially increase our sampling of orbital architectures in a critical region of the Neptunian parameter space, and will provide the stellar and planetary communities with spatially-resolved stellar spectra and a catalog of Neptune candidates for atmospheric follow-up with the JWST and ground-based spectrographs.

Title: Peter Pan, runaways, or isolated births? Unveiling the nature of the dispersed young stellar population with SOXS
Abstract: Gaia XP spectra have revealed a large, previously unrecognised population of accreting young stellar objects (YSOs) located far from known star-forming regions. Their nature is unknown: they may be long-lived "Peter Pan" YSOs dispersed into the field, young stars ejected from star-forming sites, or the product of isolated in-situ star formation, which would challenge the clustered star formation paradigm. We propose SOXS spectroscopy of 161 of these YSOs within 200pc, all targeted by an approved ALMA survey measuring their disk masses. The simultaneous near-UV to near-IR coverage of SOXS will deliver stellar parameters, extinctions, ages, accretion rates from the Balmer jump, the Li I youth indicator, and radial velocities for 3D kinematics. Together with ALMA, these data will reveal the origin of this population, test disk evolution outside clustered environments, and calibrate Gaia XP spectra as a YSO diagnostic. As the targets are spread across the sky, this is an ideal SOXS filler.

Title: Testing for environmentally regulated  stellar accretion rates in Taurus
X-Shooting the Gold Sample of Herbig stars
Abstract: Herbig stars are intermediate-mass young stars surrounded by protoplanetary disks, offering a key laboratory for star and planet formation between the T Tauri and massive young star regimes. A “Gold Sample” constituted by the complete population of Herbig stars within 300 pc has been recently identified. Yet ~ 30 % of them lack broad-band spectroscopy. We propose to observe these 19 targets with X-Shooter, which will allow us to provide robust measurements of fundamental stellar parameters, accretion rates, and emission-line diagnostics of accretion and winds. Combined with similar X-Shooter-based data for the rest of the Gold Sample, results from this proposal will establish a homogeneous spectroscopic legacy for the whole nearby Herbig population, which is crucial to tackle long-standing problems like the early evolution of intermediate-mass stars, the unexpectedly extended disk lifetimes, the transition between accretion modes, and the connection between disks and planetary systems.

Title: How Much Time Do Planets Have To Form? The Effect of External Photoevaporation on the Disk Lifetime
Abstract: Planets form in disks around low-mass stars. The disk lifetime is necessary for models of planet formation, yet it appears to vary widely between regions, due to survey sensitivity and physical effects like external photoevaporation. Most stars and planets form in massive star-forming regions where this destroys the planet-forming disks. Existing disk lifetime measurements target nearby, low-mass clusters or massive stars in more distant regions, causing significant bias. An unbiased comparison measures the surviving disk fraction in a consistent mass range across regions. We propose to make this critical measurement with wide-field HAWK-I J-, H-, and K-band images of the massive cluster Pismis 24. When combined with archival data, we will identify cluster members and measure the mass-limited disk fraction as a function of UV radiation. This is an essential test of the environmental dependence of the disk fraction to resolve the intra-cluster disk fraction tension in the literature.

Title: Nature or Nurture? Using Accretion Timescales to Investigate Depleted Disks in Corona Australis
Abstract: A major hurdle in understanding planet formation is that the physical processes driving disk evolution remain poorly constrained. Studying relations among stellar and disk properties offers a promising avenue to constrain disk evolution mechanisms, but these must be investigated across different regions to account for age and environmental effects. The young Corona Australis (CrA) region is particularly intriguing: ALMA surveys reveal disks with masses comparable to those in much older populations, challenging conventional models of disk dispersal. To test whether CrA disks were born with small reservoirs or are evolving unusually fast, we propose VLT/X-Shooter observations to measure accretion depletion timescales (Mdisk/Macc) for 15 CrA sources with ALMA disk-mass estimates. This program will deliver the first statistically robust assessment of accretion in CrA, enabling direct comparison with other regions and clarifying the origin of its depleted disks.

Title: The next frontier. A study on the nature of a newly identified population of forming stars in the Galaxy
Abstract: Gaia XP spectra have revealed a large, previously unrecognised population of low-accreting Young Stellar Objects (YSOs) overlooked in earlier surveys.  This new population is mostly spatially dispersed, located away from classical star-forming regions. The nature of these YSOs is uncertain: they may be long-lived YSOs, recently ejected stars, or evidence for in-situ isolated star formation. To distinguish between these scenarios, we propose X-Shooter spectroscopy of the complete, volume-limited sample of 103 Gaia-identified YSOs within 200 pc. X-Shooter uniquely enables simultaneous measurements of Li I absorption (a proxy of age), mass accretion rates, and radial velocities. These data will clarify the nature of this dispersed population and complete our view of star formation in the local Galaxy. This survey will deliver a legacy dataset of immense archival value, advancing models of protoplanetary disk and planet formation, while calibrating the XP spectra for the upcoming Gaia DR4.

Title: The role of the environment on mass accretion in the Orion Nebula
Abstract: Ultimately understanding planet and star formation, requires knowing how pre-main sequence (PMS) stars accrete mass. Our recent photometric study of PMS in the Orion Nebula suggests that Macc correlates with stellar and ISM densities, indicating potential environmental effects on disc evolution, beyond external UV radiation. We propose to obtain X-Shooter observations of 77 PMS in Orion within two distinct density regimes: high-density (>100 stars/pc², dense ISM) and low-density (<10 stars/pc², no ISM). The spectroscopic data across UV-optical-NIR wavelengths will provide accurate measurements of stellar parameters, extinction, and accretion properties through multiple diagnostics. The observations will allow us to quantify how the stellar and ISM density influence protoplanetary disc evolution. This study will quantify the for environmental impact on disc accretion, advancing our understanding of planetary system formation in different environments.

Title: Capturing dusty winds in the Orion proplyds
Abstract: The tremendous advancement in the characterization of exoplanetary systems is revealing a wide diversity in their bulk properties. Surveys of protoplanetary disks are leading to first attempts in comparing properties of the planet formation environments to the observed exoplanets. However, the majority of stars and detected exoplanets has formed in highly irradiated environments, within massive stellar clusters. Similar conditions can be found in the centre of the Orion Nebula Cluster. We propose to image 8 proplyds at high angular resolution (~40 mas, 16 au) at the center of the ONC with SPHERE. These observations will trace whether micron-size dust particles are entrained in the photoevaporative winds, removing dust mass from the planet forming regions. The synergy of MUSE NFM and ALMA data will reveal how the dust entrainment correlates with the evaporative mass loss rates and with the disk properties, allowing for long-awaited constraints on photoevaporative models.

Title: Completing JWST: VISIR observations of evolved stars in Westerlund 1
Abstract: The late evolution of massive stars involves material ejection through winds and outflows. Despite their importance for the evolution of the star itself and the influence of their environment, our understanding of the mass ejection is still limited. JWST MIRI observations serendipitously detected multiple winds from evolved stars in Westerlund 1, the most massive young star cluster in the Galaxy. This allows a comparative study of winds from a coeval sample of stars. However, the MIRI observations are saturated even in the shortest exposure. Here we propose VISIR broad band imaging in similar bands as the MIRI observations to retrieve the information of the winds in the closest vicinity of the stars. Interesting in their own rights, the VISIR observations will release the full potential of the JWST data. The sample of eight stars can be covered with six VISIR pointings.

Title: Confirming the environmental impact on mass accretion in the Orion Nebula
Abstract: We propose X-Shooter observations of pre-main sequence (PMS) stars in the Orion Nebula to investigate how environmental factors influence mass accretion rates (Macc). Our photometric study revealed that Macc correlate with stellar and ISM densities, suggesting potential environmental effects on disc evolution. We will observe 77 PMS stars from two distinct density regimes: high-density (41 stars, >100 stars/pc² and dense ISM) and low-density (36 stars, <10 stars/pc²). The spectroscopic data across UV-optical-NIR wavelengths will provide accurate measurements of stellar parameters, extinction, and accretion properties through multiple diagnostics. By targeting stars at varying distances from ionising sources, we will quantify how the ISM density and external UV radiation influence protoplanetary disc evolution. This study will provide definitive evidence for environmental impact on disc accretion, advancing our understanding of planetary system formation in different environments.

Title: MUSE exploration of intermediate-UV radiation in sigma Orionis: testing disk evolution using proplyds
Abstract: The multitude of exoplanets we know are still awaiting an explanation of how they were born. Understanding how planets form requires a detailed knowledge of their birth environments, the protoplanetary disks. It is known that the effect of external photoevaporation due to high energy UV radiation from massive stars at the center of young stellar clusters plays a significant role in shaping the disk sizes and in shortening their lifetimes, and thus the timescale of planet formation. Yet, after multiple studies in the high-UV environment of the young (1-2 Myr) Orion Nebula Cluster, many open questions are still remaining, especially about the effect of intermediate-UV environments and at late stages of disk evolution. With the unique capabilities of MUSE, we will measure externally-induced photoevaporation rates and lifetimes of protoplanetary disks in sigma Orionis (~3-5 Myr), and therefore constrain disk photoevaporation physics in a still unexplored part of the UV-age parameter space.

Title: Targeting a key signature of external photoevaporation with MUSE-NFM
Abstract:
Studying the evolution of protoplanetary disks is the key to understand the processes shaping planetary systems and the observed exoplanet diversity. Most planetary systems, including our Solar System, formed in massive star clusters where UV radiation from OB stars drives external photoevaporation. Proplyds, externally photoevaporating disks, are known to exhibit forbidden emission lines which trace both internal and external photoevaporation. 
Thanks to the advent of MUSE-NFM, a tracer for solely externally launched winds, [CI] at 8727 A, has been identified in proplyds in the Orion Nebula Cluster. The [CI] emission is extremely rare in low-mass star-forming regions compared to massive clusters, and could change how the physical conditions of winds are determined in these systems. We propose to observe eight proplyds with MUSE-NFM, which also have disk properties available from ALMA data. This will allow us to study [CI] in a larger sample than the previous six overlapping targets.

Title: Measuring disk fractions in massive star-forming regions
Abstract: Planets form in disks around low-mass stars. A key constraint for planet formation models is the disk lifetime. In order to truly constrain the disk lifetime, a better test is to measure the surviving disk fraction around low-mass stars in a massive region. We propose to make this critical measurement with wide-field near-IR images of all massive clusters within 2 kpc using HAWK-I; we request 3 clusters in P115. We request J-, H-, K-band, and Br-gramma images. When combined with data available in the literature and/or archive, we will identify cluster members and measure the surviving disk fraction. Results will provide an essential constraint on how much external photoevaporation reduces the planet-formation timescale in typical environments.

Title: Disk survival in typical star/planet forming conditions
Abstract: Most stars and planets form in massive and relatively dense clusters but most studies have focused on low-mass regions. In massive regions, external ionization from nearby high-mass stars truncates and destroys planet-forming disks and formed planetary systems. Models are beginning to include feedback from the environment but observations are lacking. Therefore, we propose to map 2 massive clusters with MUSE and 1 with HAWK-I to provide a statistical sample down to the low-mass population of these more typical star forming environments. With the spatial and spectral sampling of integral-field-unit (IFU) spectroscopy, we will determine: spectral types, accretion rates, ages, stellar kinematics, nebular excitation, and extinction. We target a range of densities and FUV fluxes over which external photoevaporation significantly impacts disks. Data and outputs from this program will provide significant legacy value to the community, including identifying prime targets for the ELT.

Title: Spectrally resolving the [CI]8727, 9824, and 9850 AA lines with UVES to decipher external photoevaporation
Abstract:
The effect of external photoevaporation from massive stars on the evolution of protoplanetary disks must be deciphered to understand how a system like our own did form and evolve. We have long been studying prototypical disks in massive star-forming environments, known as proplyds, targeting forbidden emission lines known to trace both internal as well as external photoevaporation. Thanks to the advent of MUSE-NFM, images of proplyds have been taken at all optical forbidden emission lines, revealing the potential of a new external photoevaporation tracer, the [CI] lines. These lines are extremely rarely detected in low-mass star-forming regions, and could be a tell-tale tracer of external photoevaporation and a potentially game changer in the determination of the physical conditions of winds in these systems.
Here we propose to observe these lines with UVES at 3 km/s resolution to measure their width and peak velocity to confirm the origin in a slow externally photoevaporated wind.

Title: Targeting a key signature of external photoevaporation with MUSE NFM

Title: Characterizing the host stars of proto-planetary disks in extreme radiation environments
Abstract: Our knowledge of the formation history of planetary systems is obtained by comparing the demographics of proto-planetary disks in nearby low-mass star forming regions with the exoplanetary system population. However, it is well known that most stars form in environments exposed to much stronger far-UV (FUV) radiation and therefore, it is questionable that the well studied population of planet forming disks is representative of those in which most exoplanets were assembled. We propose FORS2 red spectroscopic observations to study 14 proto-planetary disks in varying degree of FUV field strengths in the HII region NGC 6357.  These observations will be complemented by recently completed cycle 1 JWST-MIRI program providing 5-28 micron spectroscopy. The FORS2 spectra will provide the missing, but highly desirable, stellar parameters of the host stars allowing an assessment of internal vs external evaporation and better fitting of the disk emission.

Title: Determining the cooling timescale in a shadowed protoplanetary disk
Abstract: The planetary systems detected so far show a great diversity in their architectures, which may originate from the variety of initial conditions for their formation in protoplanetary disks. Disks evolve through a variety of mechanisms, such as planet formation and (magneto-)hydrodynamical instabilities. Theoretical models of these processes and interpretation of disk observations however require strong assumptions to be made on fundamental and unknown disk properties, such as the gas mass and the temperature structure. In this proposal, we aim to observationally measure the cooling timescale of a shadowed protoplanetary disk by obtaining nearly contemporaneous observations of a shadowed disk with SPHERE and ALMA.

Title: Direct imaging of protoplanet candidates driving kinematic signatures in disks
Abstract: ALMA is now performing the most sensitive search for protoplanet candidates as traced by planet-disk interaction signatures in the gas velocity field of their natal protoplanetary disks. In six sources, the disk gas substructure and its kinematics provide strong evidence of embedded protoplanet candidates. We propose to use the new high contrast imaging capabilities of the VLT/ERIS instrument to directly image the inferred giant protoplanets in their L-band thermal emission. The long wavelength will dramatically reduce the impact of circumstellar and circumplanetary extinction along the line of sight to the planets, significantly improving current searches in the short NIR. These deep searches will (1) confirm the planetary nature of the kinematic features observed at sub-mm wavelengths, and (2) place initial constraints on the luminosity of the protoplanets. These goals are the critical first steps in developing comprehensive follow-up observations of these protoplanets.

Title: The orbit and inner disk structure of young stellar encounters with VLTI/GRAVITY
Abstract: The formation of young T Tauri Stars (TTS) involve complex interplay between their environment, and in particular with stellar multiplicity, which in turn impacts the process of planet formation. Still, dynamical encounter in young multiple systems are difficult to constrain quantitatively, in particular due to our lack of knowledge of the orbit of these objects and the complete geometry of the inner and outer disk. We propose to the unique capability of VLTI/GRAVITY to measure the astrometry of two well-known multiple systems, HT Lup and AS205,  and constrain the morphology of the disk. These observations will be compared to the astrometry obtained with adaptive optics and ALMA to constrain the orbit of all components, and with the substructures and disk dynamics observed with ALMA, in particular disk misalignment. Together, the accurate orbit and the inner disk uniquely probed by GRAVITY will be crucial to provide a global coherent picture of the encounter and its dynamics.

Title: Bringing planet formation home: a MUSE survey of the typical birthplace of stars and planets
Abstract: The majority (>50%) of stars form in clusters/associations where they will be affected by feedback from neighboring stars. This is particularly important for planet formation as feedback from high-mass stars accelerates the destruction of planet-forming disks, contributes elements that affect geochemistry, and alters the architecture of planetary systems. While models of planet formation now include feedback from the larger star-forming environment, there is a lack of observations to compare these models to. We propose to solve this problem by surveying 6 high-mass star-forming clusters with MUSE to provide a statistical sample of low-mass stars forming in more typical environments. Our primary goal is to identify and characterise low-mass (< 1 Msun) cluster members as their disks will be most vulnerable to external feedback. The continuous spatial sampling provided by integral-field-unit (IFU) spectroscopy is essential to properly subtract bright and variable nebular emission in these regions. IFU spectroscopy is more efficient and more complete than other survey methods, enabling us to accomplish a broad range of science goals with the MUSE data alone. With the broad spectral coverage of MUSE we will determine: spectral types, accretion and outflow rates, ages and age gradients, stellar kinematics, and nebular excitation. We target regions with a range of densities and FUV fluxes to sample the conditions where external photoevaporation is expected to lead to significant destruction of planet-forming disks. As such, the outputs of this programme and the dataset it will produce will provide significant legacy value to the community. Finally, low-mass stars in high-mass regions will be prime targets for the ELT. It is essential to lay the ground-work now to identify the best targets for resolved observations to measure the impact of high-mass stars on exoplanet demographics.

Title: MUSE NFM observations of proplyds in the Orion Nebula Cluster: the key to understand disk winds
Abstract: Several processes affect the evolution of protoplanetary disks and, in turn, their ability to form planets. Therefore, a detailed understanding of the impacts of external photoevaporation is key to constraining planet formation scenarios. Here we want to follow up on the first spatially and spectrally resolved images of protoplanetary disks in the harsh environment of the Orion Nebula Cluster obtained with the unprecedented MUSE NFM IFU data. Resolving and empirically constraining external photoevaporation is mandatory to be able to bridge the gap to the study of the more distant and massive regions, where disks are unresolved but environmental conditions are more similar to the birth environment of planets.

The X-shooter spectra and FORS2 imaging will provide the stellar properties, extinction, accretion rates and inner disk sizes.  These observations will be complemented by an approved JWST-MIRI program providing 5-28 micron spectroscopy. Both datasets will provide a detailed understanding of the evolution of proto-planetary disks in extreme radiation environments.

Title: Dust entrainment in a photoevaporative wind
Abstract: External photoevaporation is thought to play an important role in protoplanetary disk evolution and dispersal, in particular in regions with strong ambient radiation fields, such as the Orion Nebula Cluster (ONC).  Furthermore, models predict that photoevaporative winds can lead to significant mass loss rates if grain growth is in place in the disk. We propose to observe with MUSE in NFM the well known dd114-426 protoplanetary disk, seen in silhouette against the bright ONC background. The proposed observations will allow us to: (1)  measure dust grain size studying the extinction of the bright background emission by the dust grains present in the translucent disk; (2) use the [OI] line, to kinematically prove that the disk is photoevaporated; (3) as a consequence, prove for the first time that photoevaporative winds can entrain dust grains, and provide constraints on the mass loss rate predicted by theoretical models.  MUSE (in NFM) is the best and only instrument to allow this study.

Title: Measuring mass loss rates of proplyds in the intermediate UV-radiation field of NGC1977 with MUSE
Abstract: The evolution of protoplanetary disks and their ability to form planets is regulated by several processes. This is a well known effect in massive clusters, like the ONC. Lower-UV radiation fields are instead expected in the majority of planet-forming young stellar clusters. We propose here to use MUSE NFM spatially and spectrally resolved observations of the 4 known proplyds in the NGC1977 cluster observable with MUSE to measure the mass loss rate due to photoevaporation in this low-UV radiation environment. We will demonstrate or disprove that considerable mass-loss occurs in low UV-radiation environments, and constrain the models of external photoevaporation.

Title: MUSE exploration of very low-UV radiation in sigma Orionis: testing disk evolution using proplyds
Abstract: Surveys of young stars with disks using ALMA and spectroscopy are giving us a detailed view of disk evolution and, in turn, planet formation. Recent observations and theoretical works are showing that the effect of external photoevaporation due to high energy ultraviolet radiation from massive stars at the center of young stellar clusters plays a significant role in shaping the disk sizes and in shortening their lifetimes, therefore shortening the timescale available to form planets. Previous studies seeking to directly probe externally-induced disk winds have focussed on young star-forming regions; we instead target the intermediate age (3-5 Myr) sigma Orionis cluster. With the unique capabilities of MUSE, we will measure externally-induced photo-evaporation rates and lifetimes of protoplanetary disks in sigma Orionis, and therefore constrain disk physics in a massive, intermediate-aged cluster. This is a unique opportunity to shed light on the mechanism powering accretion in disks.

Title: Probing the external photoevaporation of planet-forming discs with CI
Abstract: Planets form in stellar clusters where the UV environment can deplete and truncate the planet-forming circumstellar disc. For a long time we have only been able to observe this "external photoevaporation" in the most extreme UV environments like the Orion Nebula Cluster, where  unsubtle cometary plumes are launched from the disc. However such winds have been difficult to observe since in that case the system may not have a cometary morphology and much of the wind is photodissociation dominated, which cannot be traced by molecules like CO. Conversely, CI is predicted to provide unambiguous signatures of these photoevaporative winds in weak/intermediate UV environments. We propose to use nFLASH for a pilot study to verify this, observing CI 3P1-3P0 emission from the small number of known evaporating discs at the high end of intermediate UV regime.

Title: Probing protoplanetary disk survivability in the harsh environment of the Orion Nebula Cluster with MUSE NFM
Abstract: Several processes affect the evolution of protoplanetary disks and, in turn, their ability to form planets. In particular, external photoevaporation of disks driven by the UV radiation from OB stars at the center of stellar clusters is predicted to severely shorten disk lifetimes. Such environments are considered the birthplace for many planetary systems, including our own Solar System. Therefore, a detailed understanding of the impacts of external photoevaporation is key to constraining planet formation scenarios. Here we want to follow up on the first spatially and spectrally resolved images of protoplanetary disks in the harsh environment of the Orion Nebula Cluster obtained with the unprecedented MUSE NFM IFU data. We will provide the first estimates of the mass loss rate of these objects using the resolved kinematic and physical properties obtained with MUSE, in combination with published ALMA estimates of disk radii. From the disk masses we will derive their expected lifetimes.

Title: Probing the external photoevaporation of planet-forming discs with CI
Abstract:
Planet formation happens in stellar clusters where the UV environment can deplete and truncate the planet-forming circumstellar disc. For a long time we have only been able to observe this "external photoevaporation" in the most extreme UV environments, where  unsubtle cometary plumes are launched from the disc (as for the proplyds in the Orion Nebula Cluster). Recently, Kim et al. (2016) found proplyds using H alpha, in an intermediate UV environment. However more observations and tracers are required to characterise the wind and to identify evaporation in even weaker UV regimes. 

A recent prediction from state of the art models is that CI is an excellent tracer of these photoevaporative winds in weak/intermediate UV environments. We propose to use nFLASH to study CI 3P1-3P0 emission from the Kim et al. (2016) proplyds. This will  both kinematically probe these winds and demonstrate the power of CI for probing external photoevaporation for the first time
